text.p: Romanian Prime Minister- designate Victor Ciorbea presented on Monday the list of his new cabinet and signalled reformist measures in a government programme which parliament will discuss this week.
Parliament is expected to debate the list of the centrist cabinet and its programme in a joint sesion on Tuesday.

President Emil Constantinescu named Ciorbea last month after his centrist Democratic Convention (CDR) won the November 3 parliamentary elections, ousting the leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), to form a cabinet with the Social Democratic Union (USD) and the Hungarian Democratic Union (UDMR).

Analysts welcomed the new government's programme, but warned that the economic hardships inherited from the PDSR, which stalled reforms during its four years in power, would make difficult the radical surgery Romania's economy needs.
"The programme highlights a new spirit in Bucharest, a clear orientation to the market economy and the deepening of reforms," independent analyst Ilie Serbanescu told Reuters.
Under a short-term programme, the new cabinet will take steps to boost economic reforms, control the budget gap, fight poverty and unemployment and stimulate foreign investments.
Ensuring funds for energy imports and resuming talks with the International Monetary Fund on blocked credits as well as completing a 1991 land reform are also part of the package.

"I think it would be wrong to call the new government other than reformist," a Western political analyst said. "The new team is reformist in intentions. They will have to start thinking of what previously was unthinkable about reforms."

"Reform in Romania, which has been carried out so far on the surface of the economy, must target enterprises now," Serbanescu said. "Reform is more difficult at that level as it involves large economic and social costs."
The CDR, the USD and the UDMR hold 287 of parliament's 486 seats. They signed a coalition accord last week pledging to support the new cabinet and its economic programme.

The list showed Ciorbea entrusted key ministerial jobs in the proposed cabinet to representatives of the main National Peasant Party, the backbone of the CDR bloc, and to the former ministers of reform, justice and transport who served in the cabinet led by ex-prime minister and USD leader Petre Roman.
"Some ministers bring with them the good legacy and the good lessons of their previous experience and this is positive," the Western analyst said.
Roman, Romania's first post-communist prime minister, was ousted in 1991 by rioting miners who opposed his reforms.
The new cabinet also includes representatives of the UDMR, a party standing for the interests of 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians -- a first in Romania's post-Communist history.
